items.readable_text:
Content:
The side-side-side (SSS) similarity criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are similar. It states the following:

Content:
> Two triangles are similar if the ratios of the lengths of their corresponding sides are equal.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the triangles below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9aef0cc1e1bcfb45976b1fed48b415a0]

Content:
Let's check the ratios of the corresponding sides:

Content:
[MATH: (AB)/(EF)|= (3)/(6) = (1)/(2); (BC)/(FG)|= (4)/(8) = (1)/(2); (CA)/(GE)|= (2)/(4) = (1)/(2)]

Content:
The ratios are all equal, so according to the SSS criterion, the two triangles are similar:

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG.]

  • [MATH: \mathcal{Q}] is not similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SSS since the ratios of the lengths of the corresponding sides are not equal: [MATH: \dfrac{12}{8} eq\dfrac{10}{6} eq\dfrac{8}{4}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \mathcal{P}] only."

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Consider triangles [MATH: \triangle BAC] and [MATH: \triangle ACD .] Let's calculate the ratios of corresponding sides: [MATH: (AB)/(AC)|= (8)/(6) = (4)/(3); (BC)/(AD)|= (4)/(3); (AC)/(CD)|= (6)/(4.5) = (4)/(3)]

Since the ratios are equal, we conclude that [MATH: \triangle BAC\sim\triangle ACD] by the SSS criterion. Therefore, [MATH: ∠ACD≅∠CAB.]

Now, since the angles [MATH: \angle ACD] and [MATH: \angle CAB] are congruent, they are alternate interior angles, and we have

[MATH: \overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}.]

Therefore, the consecutive interior angles [MATH: \angle ABC] and [MATH: \angle BCD] are supplementary, and we obtain the following:

[MATH: m∠BCD + m∠ABC|= 180^{∘}; m∠BCD + 47^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠BCD|= 133^{∘}]
